newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Devaluation debate heats up again in Argentina.
newsitem.headline: Devaluation debate heats up again in Argentina.

text.p: Like an old scar that never heals, talk of a devaluation of the local peso currency has erupted again in Argentina.
The debate was triggered by powerful businessman Jorge Born, who said recently the current convertibility system makes Argentine companies less competitive abroad.
"Average wages in dollars are too high," said Born, head of the multinational Bunge y Born.

He was joined in calling for an exchange rate change by two former government advisors, the leader of the center-right Democratic Center Union party Alvaro Alsogaray and economist Guillermo Calvo, although each had different formulas.

"The time is approaching when pressures will require a solution to the problem that must be tackled together by economists, businessmen and the government so as not to alarm the population," said Alsogaray.

The Argentine peso has been pegged at parity to the dollar by law since April of 1991 under the convertibility plan designed by former Economy Minister Domingo Cavallo, which guarantees virtually full backing of the currency in gold, dollars and bond reserves.
Convertibility was highly successful in taming once runaway inflation, which this year will be around zero percent, but some analysts say it prevented Argentina from becoming a leading exporter.
Market sources told Reuters a powerful U.S. bank based in Argentina was conducting research into the possible repercussions of a devaluation of up to 30 percent.
As rumours spread this week, President Carlos Menem came out denying "any possibility of a devaluation."
Most analysts think the exchange rate has distorted relative prices, favoring producers of goods sold only in the country and hurting exports.
But although there is a near-consensus regarding the disease, the cure is shrouded in controversy.

"A nominal devaluation is not the solution. It would create such chaos that it would be impossible for it to affect real variables," said economist Juan Carlos de Pablo, a staunch supporter of the convertibility plan.

In a similar vein economist Aldo Abram of consultants Proeco said: "If relative prices are really distorted, the way out is not a devaluation but a deregulation of the markets and flexibilization of labor laws."
The government recently proposed sweeping labor reforms.
For his part leading economist and former economy minister Roberto Alemann warned: "Even the mere hint of a devaluation would leave banks without a single peso deposit."
Government economists dismiss talk that exports are suffering, noting they have surged to $21 billion in 1995 from $12 billion in 1991 and could reach $28 billion this year.
Critics of peso-dollar parity say exports still account only for eight percent of gross domestic product against an average 16 percent in other Latin American countries.
But even the harshest critics agree a devaluation is made more difficult by the fact that three million people have dollar debts and public utility rates are fixed in dollars.

"This is the poison pill that Cavallo left us and will be suffered by all Argentines," said economist Eduardo Conessa. "A devaluation would cause savers to go broke and many Argentines would be unable to pay their utility bills."
-- Buenos Aires Newsroom 541 318-0654
